title: Memphis Light, Gas and Water Division v. Craft (1978)
shortTitle: Memphis Light, Gas and Water Division v. Craft (1978)
summary: Before a municipal utility cuts off service over a disputed bill, due process requires notice that tells the customer how to contest the bill and an opportunity to present the dispute to an employee who can correct errors.
notes:
Key line: "Utility service is a necessity of modern life; indeed, the discontinuance of water or heating for even short periods of time may threaten health and safety." (Powell, J.)

Citation: 436 U.S. 1 (1978).

sections.Parties: The petitioners were Memphis Light, Gas and Water Division, a division of the city of Memphis, Tennessee, that supplies utility service, and its president and general manager, vice president, members of its Board of Commissioners and two employees responsible for terminating service, sued in their official and personal capacities. The respondents were Willie S. Craft and Mary Craft, homeowners at 1019 Alaska Street in Memphis, the only remaining plaintiffs from a group of customers who had sued under 42 U.S.C. section 1983 for declaratory and injunctive relief and damages. The district court dismissed the utility itself as not a person under section 1983, and that ruling was not reviewed.
sections.Material Facts: When the Crafts moved into their house in October 1972 it had two sets of gas and electric meters left from its use as a duplex; the seller said the second set was inoperative. In 1973 they began receiving two bills, one under the name Willie C. Craft, each with a separate city service fee. In October 1973 a meter reader told them both sets were running, and they hired a contractor to combine the meters, but he did the work improperly and double billing continued until January 1974. During that period their service was terminated five times for nonpayment. Mrs. Craft repeatedly missed work to visit the utility's offices, but no one explained the cause or told her of any procedure for disputing a bill. The utility's final notice said only that payment was overdue and service would be discontinued. The utility processed about 33,000 high bill complaints in 1973 but never distributed a description of any dispute procedure.
sections.Procedural History: In February 1974 the Crafts and other customers sued in the District Court for the Western District of Tennessee. After trial the court refused to certify a class and entered judgment for the defendants, although it found that the procedure for talking with management had not been adequately explained to Mrs. Craft and suggested a $35 credit. The Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed the denial of class certification but held that the procedures accorded the Crafts did not comport with due process, 534 F.2d 684 (1976). The Supreme Court granted certiorari on February 22, 1977, 429 U.S. 1090, and affirmed on May 1, 1978. The utility abandoned its argument that no state action was present.
sections.Issue: Three questions were decided. Whether the case was moot after the billing problem had been cleared up during the litigation. Whether a customer of a municipal utility has a property interest in continued service protected by the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. And, if so, whether the utility deprived the Crafts of property without due process by giving a termination notice that did not mention any way to contest the bill and by failing to provide an opportunity to present the dispute to a responsible employee before service was cut off, or whether available common law remedies were enough.
sections.Holding: The case was not moot because the Crafts' claim for actual and punitive damages remained. Under Tennessee decisional law a utility may terminate only for nonpayment of a just bill and not at will, so the Crafts had a legitimate claim of entitlement protected by the Due Process Clause. The utility deprived them of that interest without due process. Notice of termination that does not tell the customer of an available procedure for protesting an unjustified cutoff is constitutionally inadequate, and due process requires at a minimum an opportunity to present a complaint of overcharge to designated personnel empowered to correct errors before service is terminated. The judgment of the Sixth Circuit was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Powell relied on Tennessee cases, especially Trigg v. Middle Tennessee Electric Membership Corp., which recognized an exception to a utility's right to cut off service when the customer has a bona fide dispute about the bill. Because termination was allowed only for cause, the interest was property under Board of Regents v. Roth. On notice, the Court applied Mullane: the final notice warned the Crafts to pay or face termination but was not reasonably calculated to inform them of an opportunity to present objections, and the opportunity to meet with management, if it existed, depended on word of mouth referral. Lay consumers of an essential service should be told where, when and before whom disputed bills may be considered. On the hearing, the Court applied the three Mathews v. Eldridge factors. The customer's interest was self-evident because utility service is a necessity of modern life; the risk of error was not insubstantial given reliance on computers; and the utility's burden was slight, because a meeting with a responsible employee could be scheduled during the thirty days between billing and cutoff. Common law remedies did not cure the defect: cessation of utility service works a uniquely final deprivation, and the sums involved are too small to justify counsel or a lawsuit. An informal administrative remedy of this kind was the process that was due.

topics.lrs-o-due-process-framework: The court rejected judicial remedies as a substitute for an accessible opportunity to resolve the disputed bill before utility termination.
topics.lrs-o-new-property: The property interest arose from a state-law entitlement to utility service absent cause for termination.

learning.separateOpinions: The vote was 6 to 3. Justice Stevens dissented, joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justice Rehnquist. He agreed that Tennessee law gave the customer a legitimate claim of entitlement, but argued that the record showed no constitutional defect: the Division terminated about 2,000 customers a month after notices carrying an information center telephone number answered by 30 or 40 employees who could delay cutoffs and refer callers to credit counselors, a homeowner need not be told how to complain about a bill, and a customer can always avoid termination by paying the disputed amount and seeking a refund. He said the Court's holding trivialized procedural due process.
